html:
My cousin and his family leave tomorrow, which brings our five-day mahjong festival at Second Aunt’s, his mother’s place, to a close. We set off the day after tomorrow.

At last I’m going back to normal life, and I’m really looking forward to it. At the same time, three months of living under one roof with my parents, at my place, are about to begin. I was just chatting with my childhood friend, who said things at home were in such chaos that he, his wife and their kid went to Thailand for New Year, leaving his mother to hold the fort. What gives me some confidence is that, compared with other parents, mine don’t have much of a generation gap with me. They are willing to try and accept new things, they think of what’s best for us, they rarely comment on our affairs, and mostly they’re supportive. So, all in all, I feel optimistic.

It was foggy today, and the smoke from the firecrackers added a bit of smog. It snowed a little in the morning, and outside the trees were coated in rime. After a few rounds of mahjong, I went out into the countryside to take photos with my cousin, his sister, his wife and their son. Our first stop was Shuishangpiao, “Skimming the Water,” a few kilometers east of my eldest aunt’s place. There’s a spring there that keeps flowing even at more than ten degrees below zero, with green grass growing in the water. I had been there in summer but never in winter, and it was magical. My cousin’s wife is a photography pro and took lots of pictures of me. In recent years I have rarely had photos taken of me on my own, and my expressions and poses were incredibly stiff. Some of us kicked trees to capture the snow falling, some took photos, some got photographed; we had a wonderful time. After leaving Shuishangpiao, we stopped wherever looked pretty to take more. The scenery today was truly beautiful; in my thirty-odd years I have rarely had the chance to see anything like it. We wound our way round to the hill behind town, took a few pictures of the pagoda, and headed home.

Back to more eating and mahjong. My cousin’s wife is four years older than me, and my nephew (my female cousin’s son) is seventeen years younger, yet I feel as if my nephew and I are the same generation. We have lots to talk about, from music to movies, from geography to history. At dinner someone at the next table was playing a video, and I said it was Jay Chou, the Taiwanese pop star. He listened for a second and immediately named the song: “In the Name of the Father.” I said, “You’ve listened to a lot of his stuff.” He doesn’t seem like a kid not yet twenty; he has the heart of a thirty-year-old. In the afternoon, when we saw something or other, I said to my cousin’s wife, “I’m just a pure passerby,” internet slang for a neutral bystander. She hesitated: “Meaning what?” It suddenly struck me that we might not be the same generation after all, even though she is only four years older. Her circle is wealthy women who travel to check in at photogenic spots, and it has little overlap with mine.
